title: Cyber threat intelligence
summary: Turn threat data into decisions: requirements and the intelligence cycle, grading sources, the Diamond Model, kill chain and ATT&CK, STIX, TAXII and MISP, bias and ACH, attribution, and writing products.
outcomes: Explain how threat intelligence differs from threat data, and write priority intelligence requirements tied to decisions
Grade sources and information with the Admiralty code and judge feeds by relevance, timeliness and unique contribution
Analyse intrusions with the Diamond Model, kill chain course-of-action matrix and ATT&CK, accounting for version changes
Represent and share intelligence with STIX 2.1, TAXII 2.1 and MISP, including confidence, markings, sightings and decay
Apply Analysis of Competing Hypotheses and recognise confirmation bias, anchoring, mirror-imaging and false flags
Judge attribution claims rung by rung, using APT1, the SolarWinds UNC2452 path and Olympic Destroyer
Read an advisory such as AA24-038A critically and write products with standard probability and confidence language

lessons.title: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for

blocks.md:
Two messages land on a Monday. The first is a file of 40,000 IP addresses from a feed, each labelled "malicious". The second is three sentences from a colleague: *a ransomware group is exploiting the VPN appliance model we run; it hit two firms in our sector last week; patch by Friday and watch VPN logins from these three addresses.*

Both are about threats. Only the second tells anyone what to do, by when, and why. **Cyber threat intelligence** (CTI) is the discipline that turns the first kind of material into the second. This course teaches how: setting the questions, collecting and grading sources, analysing with structured models, sharing in machine-readable formats, judging attribution claims, and writing a product someone acts on.

You already met intel from the consumer's side: enrichment lookups in *Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs*, the Pyramid of Pain in *Logging and detection engineering*, and enrichment pitfalls in *Security operations: alert triage and investigation*. Now you sit on the producing side.

**The standard definitions.** NIST (the US National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP 800-150, its *Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing*, separates two things:

- **Threat information**: "any information related to a threat that might help an organization protect itself against a threat or detect the activities of an actor". It includes **indicators** ("technical artifacts or observables that suggest an attack is imminent or is currently underway or that a compromise may have already occurred", such as the IP address of a command-and-control (C2) server, a domain, a file hash or an email subject line), **TTPs** (tactics, techniques and procedures: the behaviour of an actor), advisories, reports and tool configurations. An **observable** is any event, benign or malicious, on a network or system.
- **Threat intelligence**: "threat information that has been aggregated, transformed, analyzed, interpreted, or enriched to provide the necessary context for decision-making processes".

The phrase that matters is the last: intelligence supports decisions.

**Data, information, knowledge, intelligence.** The FIRST CTI curriculum (FIRST is the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams; its CTI Special Interest Group publishes a free curriculum) borrows a ladder from the Bank of England's CBEST (intelligence-led testing) guide and maps it onto the indicator types of the Lockheed Martin kill chain paper:

- **Data**: elementary facts. An IP address or email address. The kill chain paper calls these *atomic* indicators.
- **Information**: data in context, "that which reduces uncertainty". A hash or a regular expression derived from an incident: *computed* indicators.
- **Knowledge**: information applied to a problem, often as an if-then rule. *Behavioural* indicators, such as: the intruder first used a backdoor whose traffic matched a pattern at a set rate to one address, then replaced it with a file of a known MD5 hash once access was established.
- **Intelligence**: in the Cold War Hoover Commission's words quoted by FIRST, "all the things which should be known in advance of initiating a course of action".

blocks.title: From a feed entry to a decision

nodes.label:
Information
seen 2 days ago, VPN exploit

Knowledge
it hit OUR VPN logs

Intelligence
patch by Friday, hunt logins

scenes.caption: A raw feed entry is data: one address, no context. On its own it tells nobody what to do.
Processing adds context: when it was last seen and what it was tagged with. Now it reduces uncertainty a little.
Matching it against our own VPN logs turns it into knowledge about us, not about the internet in general.
An analyst adds the judgement and the recommendation: what it means, how sure we are, what to do and by when. That is intelligence.
The product succeeds only if someone decides something with it. A report that changes no decision was information, however well written.

blocks.code:
from datetime import date

# A raw feed (SYNTHETIC): indicator, type, last_seen, tag
feed = [
    ("198.51.100.7", "ip",     "2026-11-11", "vpn-exploit"),
    ("203.0.113.9",  "ip",     "2024-02-01", "spam"),
    ("bad.example",  "domain", "2026-11-09", "phishing"),
    ("198.51.100.7", "ip",     "2026-11-10", "vpn-exploit"),
]
vpn_log_sources = {"198.51.100.7", "192.0.2.10"}  # who hit our VPN this week
today = date(2026, 11, 13)

latest = {}                                   # 1. deduplicate
for value, kind, seen, tag in feed:
    d = date.fromisoformat(seen)
    if value not in latest or d > latest[value][1]:
        latest[value] = (kind, d, tag)

for value, (kind, d, tag) in sorted(latest.items()):
    age = (today - d).days                    # 2. add context
    ours = value in vpn_log_sources
    note = "IN OUR VPN LOGS" if ours else "not seen here"
    print(f"{value:<13} {tag:<11} {age:>4} days old  {note}")

# Output:
# 198.51.100.7  vpn-exploit    2 days old  IN OUR VPN LOGS
# 203.0.113.9   spam        1016 days old  not seen here
# bad.example   phishing       4 days old  not seen here
blocks.caption: Steps 1 and 2 of the ladder in code: deduplicate the feed and add context (age, and whether the address touched us). The remaining step, judgement, is the analyst's. All data is synthetic, from documentation address ranges.

blocks.md:
**Who uses CTI.** Almost every security function consumes it: the SOC (security operations centre) for triage, incident responders for scoping, detection engineers for new rules, vulnerability management for patch priority, and leaders for budget and risk decisions. FIRST's working definition captures the goal: "information about threats and threat actors [and their behaviours] that provides relevant and sufficient understanding for mitigating a potentially harmful event" in the cyber domain.

A CTI team therefore works backwards from its consumers. The next lesson shows how: by writing down the questions first.

A feed is not intelligence. 40,000 addresses with no dates, sources, context or relevance to you are data, and a lot of it is stale or shared infrastructure (recall the shared-IP and reputation-lag traps from the alert triage course). Buying more data does not produce more intelligence; analysis against a question does.
Threat intelligence is threat information that has been analysed and put in context **for a decision**. If you cannot name the decision a product supports, you are not yet producing intelligence.

blocks.question: By NIST SP 800-150's definitions, which of these is threat *intelligence* rather than threat information?
options: A list of 500 SHA-256 hashes from a malware repository
The subject line of a phishing email
An assessment that a ransomware group is exploiting the VPN model your firm runs, with a recommended patch deadline
A firewall log line showing a blocked connection
blocks.explain: NIST defines threat intelligence as threat information that has been aggregated, analysed, interpreted or enriched to give context for decision-making. Hashes, subject lines and log lines are indicators or observables: useful inputs, but nobody has yet said what they mean for you or what to do.

blocks.question: In the FIRST ladder, a rule such as: the intruder first used a backdoor beaconing to one address, then swapped it for a file with a known hash once access was established. Which level is it?
options: Knowledge (behavioural indicator)
Data (atomic indicator)
Information (computed indicator)
Not an indicator at all
blocks.explain: It combines atomic and computed indicators with sequence and logic, which is what the kill chain paper calls a behavioural indicator and FIRST maps to knowledge. It is still not intelligence until someone attaches a judgement and a recommendation for a decision.

lessons.title: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements

blocks.md:
A chief information security officer (CISO) asks the new CTI analyst: "What are the threats to us?" The analyst could spend a month reading vendor reports and still not answer, because the question supports no particular decision. Compare: "Is any ransomware group exploiting the VPN appliance model we run, and how soon after a patch is released?" That question decides something concrete: whether VPN patches get an emergency change window.

Intelligence work starts from questions like the second one, and runs in a loop called the **intelligence cycle**. FIRST's curriculum describes it as the process behind government agencies such as the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and National Security Agency (NSA), which "very broadly outlines the stages of developing raw information into finished intelligence for policy makers to use in decision making".

The phases, as the FIRST curriculum lays them out:

1. **Planning and direction**: receive, identify and prioritise intelligence requirements; task collection.
2. **Collection**: acquire the data needed to satisfy those requirements, choosing the most appropriate sources.
3. **Processing and exploitation**: convert raw collection into something analysts can use (parse, decode, translate, normalise, deduplicate).
4. **Analysis and production**: integrate, evaluate, analyse and interpret the processed information into products that satisfy the requester.
5. **Dissemination and feedback**: deliver to the right consumers and learn whether the product answered the question. Feedback becomes new direction.

It is drawn as a circle because the last step feeds the first.

blocks.title: The intelligence cycle, one requirement at a time

scenes.caption: Direction: leadership and the CTI team agree the question. PIR-1: is any ransomware group exploiting the VPN model we run?
Collection: the vendor feed, the sector sharing group and our own VPN logs are tasked against PIR-1. Collecting everything is not a plan.
Processing: deduplicate indicators, parse advisories, map vendor names for the same group onto one entry, normalise timestamps to UTC.
Analysis (a made-up example): two sector peers were hit through that VPN model within 4 days of a patch. Judgement: likely relevant to us, moderate confidence.
Dissemination: one paragraph to the CISO, a hunt request to the SOC. Feedback: the CISO now asks about our other edge devices, a new requirement.

blocks.md:
**From vague to usable.**

- Vague: "What are the threats to us?" (no decision, no scope).
- Better: "Which ransomware groups target companies like us?" (still no decision).
- Good: "Is any ransomware group exploiting the VPN appliance model we run, and how soon after patches?" Decision: whether VPN patches skip the normal monthly window.

Each PIR is then broken into concrete **information needs** that a source can actually answer, and every source you collect from should map to at least one requirement. Writing this down as a table makes gaps visible, as the script below shows.

blocks.code:
# Intelligence requirements and the sources meant to answer them (SYNTHETIC)
pirs = {
    "PIR-1": "Is any ransomware group exploiting the VPN model we run?",
    "PIR-2": "Are our customers' passwords being sold?",
    "PIR-3": "Who is targeting payment systems in our sector this quarter?",
}
sources = {
    "Vendor feed A":       {"PIR-1"},
    "Sector ISAC":         {"PIR-1", "PIR-3"},
    "Internal VPN logs":   {"PIR-1"},
    "Free IP blocklist":   set(),          # collected, but for which question?
}

for pir, question in pirs.items():
    feeding = [s for s, answers in sources.items() if pir in answers]
    status = ", ".join(feeding) if feeding else "COLLECTION GAP"
    print(f"{pir}: {len(feeding)} source(s): {status}")

for s, answers in sources.items():
    if not answers:
        print(f"Review: '{s}' answers no requirement")

# Output:
# PIR-1: 3 source(s): Vendor feed A, Sector ISAC, Internal VPN logs
# PIR-2: 0 source(s): COLLECTION GAP
# PIR-3: 1 source(s): Sector ISAC
# Review: 'Free IP blocklist' answers no requirement
blocks.caption: A collection plan as data. PIR-2 has no source at all (a collection gap to fix or to report honestly), and one feed answers no question (a cost to justify or drop). Synthetic example.

blocks.prompt: The free IP blocklist answers no PIR, but it costs nothing. Should the team keep ingesting it?
blocks.reveal: Not by default. "Free" data still costs analyst time, storage, and false positives in the SIEM. Either find the requirement it serves (for example a PIR about commodity scanning against your perimeter), or stop collecting it. NIST SP 800-150 makes the same point about indicators: "the unnecessary processing of extraneous indicators creates additional work for analysts and slows down prioritization". Requirements decide collection, not the other way round.

blocks.md:
**Dissemination is part of the job, not an afterthought.** FIRST lists four checks: the right **format** (summarise for decision makers), the right **hands** (map products to team responsibilities, not just job titles), the right **time** (relevant intelligence that arrives late is useless) and the right **medium** (the channel that reaches that stakeholder fastest).

Then ask for **feedback**: did the product answer the PIR, did anyone act, what new question does it raise? Without feedback, a CTI team cannot tell useful products from ignored ones.

The most common failure is a collection-driven programme: buy feeds, read everything, publish a weekly "threat landscape" digest that supports no decision. FIRST warns that a meeting with leadership that is "informational only" will not go well. Start from requirements and work backwards.

blocks.question: Which is the best-formed priority intelligence requirement?
options: What are all the cyber threats facing our company this year?
Tell us about ransomware.
Collect every indicator published about our sector.
Is any ransomware group exploiting the VPN appliance model we run, so we can decide whether VPN patches skip the monthly window?
blocks.explain: FIRST's three tests: one question, a specific fact or activity, one decision supported. Only the VPN question names a specific activity (exploitation of our VPN model) and the decision (emergency patching). 'All threats' and 'ransomware' are unbounded topics, and 'collect every indicator' is a collection task, not a question.

blocks.question: Two weeks after a briefing, the CISO says it was 'interesting' but nobody changed anything. In the cycle, which step most clearly failed or was skipped?
options: Collection
Planning and direction
Processing and exploitation
Encryption of the report
blocks.explain: A product that changes no decision usually answered a question nobody needed answered: the requirement was never agreed in planning and direction. Feedback (step 5) is how you discover this, but the fix is upstream: agree the PIR and the decision it serves before collecting.

lessons.title: Strategic, operational, tactical and technical intelligence

blocks.md:
The same threat needs different products for different readers. A board member deciding next year's budget needs one page on who is likely to target the company and why. A SOC analyst needs a list of domains to block before lunch. Sending the board the domain list, or the SOC the one-pager, wastes both.

CTI practice therefore sorts products into **levels** by audience, cadence and shelf life. FIRST's curriculum summarises the four levels set out in a report by MWR InfoSecurity (a UK security consultancy) and the UK's NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters), the UK signals intelligence agency):

- **Strategic**: "high level information, produced at a slower cadence, consumed by those that control the strategy of an organisation, typically executive teams or management", focused on threats that may affect business decisions.
- **Operational**: specific to the organisation and its business operations, produced faster, used "to warn defenders of an impending attack".
- **Tactical**: the TTPs (tactics, techniques and procedures) an actor uses.
- **Technical**: indicators of compromise, forensic evidence and technical descriptions, which may update firewalls and detection tools in near real time.

Naming varies between authors: many vendors fold *technical* into *tactical* and speak of three levels. When you read or write a product, check which convention the audience expects.

**Worked example: one report, four levels.** In February 2013 Mandiant, an incident response firm (later part of FireEye, now of Google), published *APT1: Exposing One of China's Cyber Espionage Units*. **APT** stands for advanced persistent threat, a label for well-resourced intruders running long campaigns; APT1 was the most prolific of the 20-plus China-based groups Mandiant tracked. The report serves every level at once:

- **Strategic**: the group is "likely government-sponsored", and the industries it targeted "match industries that China has identified as strategic to their growth", including four of seven strategic emerging industries in China's 12th Five-Year Plan.
- **Operational**: 141 victims in 20 industries since 2006, 87% headquartered in English-speaking countries; access lasted 356 days on average, 1,764 at most.
- **Tactical**: spear phishing for entry, periodic revisits to steal data, and two mail-theft tools (GETMAIL, MAPIGET) unseen elsewhere.
- **Technical**: "more than 3,000 indicators" (domains, IPs, malware MD5s) plus 13 X.509 certificates.

blocks.title: One report, four products, four readers (APT1, 2013)

scenes.caption: One piece of analysis can feed four products. The art is cutting it so each reader gets only what they act on.
Strategic: who is behind it and why, framed as business risk. It changes slowly and informs budgets, partnerships and risk acceptance.
Operational: is this campaign relevant to us, now? Targeting, timing and how long intruders stay tell the CISO whether to start a hunt.
Tactical: how they operate. Behaviours like mail-theft tooling become detections that survive new infrastructure.
Technical: machine-readable indicators go straight into blocklists and SIEM lookups. Fastest to use, fastest to go stale.

blocks.code:
# Findings from one analysis, tagged by level (figures from the APT1 report)
findings = [
    ("strategic",   "Likely state-sponsored; targets match national priority industries"),
    ("operational", "141 victims since 2006; 356-day average access"),
    ("tactical",    "Spear phishing first; GETMAIL and MAPIGET steal mail"),
    ("technical",   "3,000+ indicators: domains, IPs, MD5s, 13 certificates"),
]
readers = {"strategic": ("Board", "yearly, one page"),
           "operational": ("CISO, incident lead", "weekly brief"),
           "tactical": ("Detection engineering", "per campaign"),
           "technical": ("SOC tools", "machine feed, minutes")}

for level, (who, how) in readers.items():
    items = [text for lvl, text in findings if lvl == level]
    print(f"{who} ({how}): {len(items)} item(s)")
    for text in items:
        print("   -", text)

# Output:
# Board (yearly, one page): 1 item(s)
#    - Likely state-sponsored; targets match national priority industries
# CISO, incident lead (weekly brief): 1 item(s)
#    - 141 victims since 2006; 356-day average access
# Detection engineering (per campaign): 1 item(s)
#    - Spear phishing first; GETMAIL and MAPIGET steal mail
# SOC tools (machine feed, minutes): 1 item(s)
#    - 3,000+ indicators: domains, IPs, MD5s, 13 certificates
blocks.caption: Routing one analysis into four products: each finding is tagged with a level, and each level has its own reader and cadence. The figures are from the APT1 report; the routing table is an example.

blocks.md:
**Cadence and shelf life differ by level.** The strategic judgement in the APT1 report (a state-backed group stealing intellectual property at scale) stayed true for years. The technical annex started ageing the day it was published, and Mandiant said so itself: "publishing certain kinds of indicators dramatically shortens their lifespan", and when the unit "changes their techniques after reading this report", tracking it would get harder. The authors judged that warning many defenders at once was worth that cost.

This is the Pyramid of Pain from *Logging and detection engineering* seen from the producer's side: the cheap-to-share bottom levels are exactly the ones an exposed adversary changes first.

Write each level for its reader. Strategic: no jargon, no indicators, one recommendation per page. Operational: what, who, when, how sure, what to check. Tactical: behaviours mapped to ATT&CK with detection ideas. Technical: machine-readable files (STIX or MISP, later in this course), with dates and confidence.

blocks.question: Which product is *operational* intelligence in the MWR and NCSC sense that FIRST summarises?
options: A warning to the CISO that a group hitting two sector peers this week uses the same VPN model you run
A list of 2,000 malicious domains for the web proxy
A ten-year forecast of state-sponsored espionage trends for the board
A YARA rule for a malware family
blocks.explain: Operational intelligence is specific to the organisation and warns defenders of an impending attack. The domain list and the YARA rule are technical (or tactical, depending on convention), and the ten-year forecast is strategic.

blocks.question: Why did Mandiant expect the APT1 indicators to lose value faster than the report's strategic conclusions?
options: Because MD5 hashes expire after a year
Because strategic intelligence is classified and indicators are not
Because publishing indicators tells the adversary exactly what to change, and infrastructure and files are cheap to change
Because indicators are always wrong
blocks.explain: The report says publishing indicators 'dramatically shortens their lifespan' and expected the unit to change techniques. Domains, IPs and hashes sit low on the Pyramid of Pain, so they are cheap to replace; the organisation's mission and sponsor do not change because a report was published.

lessons.title: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth

blocks.md:
Once the requirements are written, the next question is where answers can come from. To answer PIR-1 (is anyone exploiting our VPN model?) you could read a vendor's paid feed, ask peers in a sector sharing group, read government advisories, and search your own VPN logs. Each source differs in cost, speed, coverage and how far you can trust it.

The common source types:

- **Internal telemetry and incidents**: your own logs, alerts and investigations. The most relevant source you have, because it is about you, and the only one nobody else can sell you.
- **Government advisories**: national agencies such as CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and the UK NCSC publish advisories with techniques, indicators and mitigations.
- **Sharing communities**: an **ISAC** (Information Sharing and Analysis Center) serves one sector, such as finance or health. NIST SP 800-150 defines the broader **ISAO** (Information Sharing and Analysis Organization) as "any entity or collaboration" set up by public or private organisations to gather and analyse cyber information.

- **Vendor reports and commercial feeds**: free research plus paid feeds and reports. Coverage reflects each vendor's customers and sensors.
- **OSINT** (open-source intelligence, meaning intelligence drawn from publicly available material, not from open-source software): researcher blogs, code repositories, certificate logs, domain registration data, paste sites, news.
- **Closed forums and criminal marketplaces**: sometimes the only place a stolen-credential sale appears. FIRST's curriculum advises discussing any interaction with these communities with your company's lawyers first; mature teams have written rules that protect the analyst and the company.

**What makes an indicator worth having.** NIST SP 800-150 lists five qualities. Ideally indicators are **timely** (delivered with minimal delay), **relevant** (applicable to your environment), **accurate** (correct, complete, unambiguous, with caveats stated), **specific** (describe observable events clearly enough to limit false positives) and **actionable** (enough context to decide a response).

**Measuring a source.** You cannot judge a feed by its size. A practical test is to compare each feed against indicators your own investigations confirmed as malicious, over a fixed period: how many of those did the feed contain (hits), what fraction of the feed ever touched you (hit rate), and how many hits *only* that feed had (unique contribution). The script below does this on a tiny synthetic example where each character stands for one indicator.

blocks.code:
# Which feed earns its cost? (SYNTHETIC: each character is one indicator)
feeds = {
    "A (paid)": set("abcdefghijklmnopqrst"),                  # 20
    "B (ISAC)": set("abcdwxyz"),                              # 8
    "C (free)": set("abcdefghij0123456789KLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"),  # 36
}
# Indicators seen in OUR logs and confirmed malicious by investigation
confirmed_here = set("abcwxy")

for name, f in feeds.items():
    hits = f & confirmed_here
    others = set().union(*(g for n, g in feeds.items() if n != name))
    unique = hits - others
    print(f"{name}  size {len(f):>2}  hits {len(hits)}  "
          f"hit rate {len(hits)/len(f):.0%}  unique {sorted(unique)}")

# Output:
# A (paid)  size 20  hits 3  hit rate 15%  unique []
# B (ISAC)  size  8  hits 6  hit rate 75%  unique ['w', 'x', 'y']
# C (free)  size 36  hits 3  hit rate 8%  unique []
blocks.caption: Three synthetic feeds scored against six indicators our investigations confirmed. Feed B is the smallest, yet holds every confirmed indicator the others have plus three that only it has.

scenes.caption: Hit rate: the share of each feed that matched confirmed malicious activity in our logs. Bigger feeds are not better feeds.
Unique hits as a share of our 6 confirmed indicators: only B saw w, x and y (3 of 6 = 50%). Dropping A or C would lose nothing we have seen.
Caution: 6 confirmed indicators is a tiny sample, and a feed may cover threats that simply have not reached us yet. Measure over months, against the PIRs each feed was bought for.

blocks.prompt: Feed A is paid and contributed nothing unique this quarter. Before cancelling it, what else should you check?
blocks.reveal: Whether A answers a requirement the others do not, even if it has not fired yet. A feed bought for PIR-3 (threats to payment systems) may be valuable precisely because nothing has hit you. Also check timeliness: if A delivered the shared indicators days before B, it may have bought you time. Hit counts are evidence, not the whole decision; tie the review to requirements.

blocks.md: Collect against requirements, prefer sources about you (internal telemetry, sector peers), and measure every external source by what it contributes: relevance, timeliness and unique hits, not volume. For a question like PIR-1, check CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue from *Security from zero* first.

blocks.question: Your SOC confirmed 40 malicious domains last quarter. A paid feed of 2 million domains contained 12 of them, all also present in your free ISAC feed. What does this measurement show?
options: The paid feed is the most valuable because it is the largest
The paid feed added no unique detections against what you saw last quarter; check whether it serves another requirement before renewing
The ISAC feed must be wrong because it is smaller
Both feeds should be dropped because neither had all 40
blocks.explain: Unique contribution was zero against confirmed activity, so the feed's value, if any, lies elsewhere (another PIR, earlier delivery, or threats you have not yet seen). Size says nothing about relevance, and no feed will contain everything, so missing some confirmed domains is expected.

lessons.title: Grading sources and information: the Admiralty code

blocks.md:
Two reports arrive saying the same thing: "a new phishing kit is targeting our customers". One comes from a vendor whose feeds have been accurate for years. The other comes from an account on a criminal forum that has been right before but is now contradicting several other sources. Should they carry the same weight? And if the trusted vendor's claim comes from a brand-new experimental feed, how much does its reputation help?

Intelligence services answer with a two-part grade. FIRST's curriculum recommends the model "widely used in government and some of commercial entities", usually called the **Admiralty code** or **NATO system** (NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization). FIRST calls it the NID model: the scale was developed during the Second World War by the British Admiralty's Naval Intelligence Division (NID). FIRST and the STIX specification both cite the US Army field manual FM 2-22.3 for its definitions.

**Two separate scales.** The **source** gets a letter for reliability, judged from its track record:

- **A** Reliable: no doubt about authenticity, trustworthiness or competency; history of complete reliability.
- **B** Usually reliable: minor doubts; history of mostly valid information.
- **C** Fairly reliable: doubts; has provided valid information in the past.
- **D** Not usually reliable: significant doubts.
- **E** Unreliable: history of invalid information.
- **F** Cannot be judged: not enough information to evaluate.

The **information** gets a number for credibility, judged from the content itself:

1. Confirmed: logical, consistent, confirmed by independent sources.
2. Probably true: logical and consistent, not confirmed.
3. Possibly true: reasonably logical, agrees with some information, not confirmed.
4. Doubtfully true: not logical but possible, no other information, not confirmed.
5. Improbable: not logical, contradicted by other information.
6. Cannot be judged.

blocks.title: Grading two reports on two independent scales

scenes.caption: Every report gets one letter for the source and one number for the information. The letter describes who said it; the number describes what was said.
FIRST's first example: a trusted vendor's new experimental feed. The vendor is reliable (A), but the untuned feed's data is only possibly true (3): A3.
Second example: a forum actor who is usually right (B) makes a claim that contradicts several other sources: doubtfully true (4). B4.
An unknown first-time source (F) can still send information that two independent sources confirm (1): F1. Ignoring it because the source is new would be a mistake.

blocks.md:
**Why keep the scales separate?** Because a good source can be wrong this time, and a poor or unknown source can be right. If the source's reputation is allowed to set the credibility grade, a reliable vendor's untested claim gets waved through and a newcomer's confirmed warning gets ignored. Grade the source on its history and the information on its own logic and corroboration.

**Independent means independent.** Credibility 1 requires confirmation "by independent sources". Three vendor blogs that all repeat one original report are one source, not three. This trap is called **circular reporting**. Tools can make it worse: MISP's documentation warns that when its correlation engine finds the same value in several events, "a match is a lead: it does not by itself establish maliciousness, common ownership, causality, or independent confirmation". Always trace a claim back to who actually observed it.

**Carrying grades into machine-readable formats.** STIX 2.1 (the structured threat intelligence language covered later in this course) has a single `confidence` property from 0 to 100, and its Appendix A defines a normative mapping from the Admiralty credibility scale: 1 maps to 90, 2 to 70, 3 to 50, 4 to 30, 5 to 10, and 6 to "not specified" (leave the property out). The source letter has no slot of its own in that mapping, so record the source's reliability separately, for example in the object's creator identity and your own notes.

blocks.code:
RELIABILITY = {"A": "Reliable", "B": "Usually reliable", "C": "Fairly reliable",
               "D": "Not usually reliable", "E": "Unreliable", "F": "Cannot be judged"}
CREDIBILITY = {1: "Confirmed", 2: "Probably true", 3: "Possibly true",
               4: "Doubtfully true", 5: "Improbable", 6: "Cannot be judged"}
# STIX 2.1 Appendix A: Admiralty credibility to STIX confidence (0-100)
TO_STIX = {1: 90, 2: 70, 3: 50, 4: 30, 5: 10, 6: None}

def grade(source, info):
    """Rate the source and the information separately, then combine."""
    return f"{source}{info}", RELIABILITY[source], CREDIBILITY[info], TO_STIX[info]

reports = [
    ("Trusted vendor, new experimental feed", "A", 3),
    ("Forum actor, usually right, claim contradicts others", "B", 4),
    ("Our own sensor saw it, and the IR team confirmed it", "A", 1),
]
for what, s, i in reports:
    code, rel, cred, conf = grade(s, i)
    print(f"{code}  {rel} / {cred:<16} STIX confidence {conf}  ({what})")

# Output:
# A3  Reliable / Possibly true    STIX confidence 50  (Trusted vendor, new experimental feed)
# B4  Usually reliable / Doubtfully true  STIX confidence 30  (Forum actor, usually right, claim contradicts others)
# A1  Reliable / Confirmed        STIX confidence 90  (Our own sensor saw it, and the IR team confirmed it)
blocks.caption: Grading three reports and converting the credibility digit to STIX confidence with the spec's Appendix A table. The letter and the digit are chosen independently.

blocks.md: Do not average the two grades into one number, and do not let the letter drive the digit. "A5" (a reliable source passing on something improbable) is a perfectly valid and useful grade: it tells the reader to check before acting, whoever sent it.

blocks.question: A partner CERT (computer emergency response team) with a long record of accurate reporting shares a claim that no one else has reported and that fits what you already know. What grade fits best?
options: A1
F2
B5
A2
blocks.explain: The source has a history of complete reliability (A). The claim is logical and consistent but not independently confirmed, which is 2 (probably true), not 1. F would ignore the track record, and 5 would mean the claim is contradicted.

blocks.question: Four vendor reports state that a domain belongs to the same actor. You find that all four cite one researcher's blog post. How should the credibility grade treat them?
options: As four independent confirmations: grade 1
As grade 5, because repeated claims are improbable
As one source: the four reports add reach, not independent confirmation
Grades only apply to human sources, not reports
blocks.explain: Credibility 1 needs independent confirmation. Four reports repeating one original observation are circular reporting: the evidence base is still one blog post, so grade the original claim on its own merits.

lessons.title: Indicators: types, life cycle and decay

blocks.md:
An IP address used by a phishing kit last Tuesday is a strong lead today. In a month the attacker has moved on and the address belongs to a hosting customer selling shoes. Blocking it then hurts you. Indicators have a life cycle, and a CTI team that never retires them ends up with blocklists full of noise.

**What an indicator is.** Eric Hutchins, Michael Cloppert and Rohan Amin's 2011 Lockheed Martin paper, the one that introduced the intrusion kill chain you met in *Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits*, defines an indicator as "any piece of information that objectively describes an intrusion", in three types:

- **Atomic**: cannot be broken down further and keeps its meaning: IP addresses, email addresses, vulnerability identifiers.
- **Computed**: derived from incident data: hash values, regular expressions.
- **Behavioural**: combinations of atomic and computed indicators "often subject to qualification by quantity and possibly combinatorial logic".

Behavioural indicators sit near the top of the Pyramid of Pain; atomic ones near the bottom.

**The indicator life cycle.** The same paper describes three states. Analysts **reveal** indicators through analysis or collaboration; they **mature** them by loading them into their tools; the indicators are **utilized** when matching activity is found. Investigating that activity reveals new indicators, and the loop continues.

The paper adds a warning that still applies to every feed: the cycle runs "regardless of their accuracy or applicability", so a wrong indicator also gets matured and utilized, and the noise it generates spreads. That is why every indicator needs a source, a date and a confidence attached.

blocks.title: The indicator life cycle (Hutchins, Cloppert and Amin, 2011)

scenes.caption: A partner shares a C2 domain: the indicator is revealed. Record who said it, when, and how confident they were.
You load it into the proxy blocklist and a SIEM lookup: it matures. From now on it costs something every time it matches.
A laptop resolves the domain: utilized. Investigating the laptop reveals a new hash and a second domain, and the loop turns again.
Not in the 2011 paper's figure, but essential: indicators that stop being useful must leave your tools, by age, by false-positive reports, or by an expiry date.

blocks.md: **Decay.** The Diamond Model paper (next lesson) notes that timestamps allow "a reduced confidence in knowledge over time (i.e., a decay function) as the likelihood of adversary changes increase over time". MISP, the open-source sharing platform covered later in the course, implements this as **decaying models**. Its shipped *Polynomial* model computes, within an indicator's lifetime:

blocks.caption: t is the time since the indicator was last seen or updated. The score is clamped at zero and reaches zero at the end of the lifetime; below a threshold the indicator is flagged as decayed. Base comes from taxonomy tags or a default.

blocks.title: MISP Polynomial decay: score against age

scenes.caption: Speed 0.5: the score stays high for most of the lifetime, then drops fast. The indicator is flagged decayed when the curve crosses the threshold, here a little after day 23.
Speed 2: a larger decay speed makes the score fall sooner. With the same 30-day lifetime it crosses 30 around day 12. Phishing infrastructure behaves like this.
A longer lifetime for slow-changing indicators, such as a custom malware family's hash: 60 days at speed 0.5 keeps it above the threshold for about 47 days.

blocks.code:
def decay(base, age_days, lifetime, speed, threshold):
    """MISP's Polynomial model: base x (1 - (age/lifetime)^(1/speed))."""
    if age_days >= lifetime:
        return 0.0, True
    score = base * (1 - (age_days / lifetime) ** (1 / speed))
    return round(max(score, 0.0), 1), score < threshold

# An IP from a phishing kit: base score 80, lifetime 30 days, cutoff 30
for speed in (0.5, 2):
    row = []
    for age in (0, 5, 10, 20, 29):
        s, dead = decay(80, age, lifetime=30, speed=speed, threshold=30)
        row.append(f"day {age:>2}: {s:>4}{' X' if dead else '  '}")
    print(f"speed {speed}: " + " | ".join(row))

# Output:
# speed 0.5: day  0: 80.0   | day  5: 77.8   | day 10: 71.1   | day 20: 44.4   | day 29:  5.2 X
# speed 2: day  0: 80.0   | day  5: 47.3   | day 10: 33.8   | day 20: 14.7 X | day 29:  1.3 X
blocks.caption: The same formula in Python, at two decay speeds. X marks scores below the threshold of 30, where MISP would flag the indicator as decayed.

blocks.md:
**Sightings and warning lists.** MISP records **sightings** of each attribute: type 0 means "seen", type 1 means seen and "confirmed as false-positive", type 2 means it "will be expired" at the time of the sighting. Sightings feed decay scores and tell producers which of their indicators are actually firing. MISP also ships **warning lists**: "lists of well-known indicators that can be associated to potential false positives, errors or mistakes", such as public DNS resolvers and popular domains, so a well-meaning analyst does not share 8.8.8.8 as a C2 server.

MISP's documentation adds two cautions: a decay score "does not automatically remove the attribute", and "a missing score does not mean the indicator is fresh or benign". Decay informs your review; it does not replace it.

Every indicator needs a source, a first-seen and last-seen date, and a confidence. Load it, watch what it matches, and retire it on a schedule that fits its type: days for phishing domains, longer for behaviours.

blocks.question: In MISP's Polynomial model, what happens if you raise the decay speed while keeping the same lifetime?
options: The score falls sooner within the lifetime
The indicator never decays
The lifetime doubles
The base score increases
blocks.explain: The exponent is 1/speed. A larger speed makes (t/lifetime) raised to that power approach 1 sooner, so the score drops earlier. MISP's documentation says a larger positive value 'makes the score fall sooner within the same lifetime'.

blocks.question: A colleague wants to share every IP address a sandboxed malware sample contacted, including 8.8.8.8 and a CDN address, with to_ids set to true. What is the risk, and what helps?
options: No risk: more indicators is always better
8.8.8.8 is a valid C2 indicator because the malware contacted it
Risk only if the sample is ransomware
Shared infrastructure will trigger false positives everywhere; check values against warning lists and mark context-only values as not for detection
blocks.explain: A public resolver or CDN address is contacted by benign software constantly, so blocking or alerting on it floods recipients with false positives. MISP warning lists exist to catch exactly these values, and its to_ids flag separates actionable attributes from context.

lessons.title: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners

blocks.md:
A laptop in Finance runs an unknown loader. That one fact already implies three more: someone (an adversary) used that loader (a capability) over some server or domain (infrastructure) against this laptop and its user (a victim). You know one corner; the other three are questions.

That observation is the core of the **Diamond Model of Intrusion Analysis**, published in 2013 by intrusion analysts Sergio Caltagirone, Andrew Pendergast and Christopher Betz. Its first axiom: "For every intrusion event there exists an adversary taking a step towards an intended goal by using a capability over infrastructure against a victim to produce a result." The four features are drawn at the corners of a diamond, connected by edges, which gives the model its name.

**The four core features.**

- **Adversary**: the actor responsible. The paper separates the **operator** (the person at the keyboard) from the **customer** (who benefits), which matters for intent and persistence. Usually unknown at discovery.
- **Capability**: tools and techniques, from manual password guessing to custom malware. What one capability can exploit is its *capacity*; all of them together, the *arsenal*.
- **Infrastructure**: what delivers the capability and carries command and control: IP addresses, domains, email addresses, even USB sticks. **Type 1** is owned by the adversary; **Type 2** is controlled by an intermediary, witting or not (compromised servers, hop points), and "typically, this is the infrastructure that a victim will see as the adversary".
- **Victim**: the target, split into **persona** (people, organisations) and **assets** (hosts, accounts). A victim asset can become infrastructure in a later event.

Events also have **meta-features** (timestamps, phase, result, direction, methodology, resources), and every feature has its own **confidence**.

blocks.title: Pivoting around the diamond (after the paper's Figure 5)

scenes.caption: An event has four corners and five edges. Each edge is a relationship you can exploit to find something you do not yet know.
Pivot 1: a victim discovers malware on its network. We know the victim and the capability.
Pivot 2: reversing the malware exposes its command-and-control domain. Capability leads to infrastructure.
Pivot 3: resolving the domain gives the IP address hosting the controller. We are still on the infrastructure corner, growing it.
Pivot 4: firewall logs show other internal hosts talking to that IP. Infrastructure leads back to more victims.
Pivot 5: registration details of the IP may reveal something about the adversary. Possible, never guaranteed: the paper stresses the model shows what is possible, not what is certain.

blocks.md: **Pivoting** is the paper's name for "extracting a data element and exploiting that element, in conjunction with data sources, to discover other related elements". It is hypothesis testing: each pivot finds evidence that strengthens, weakens or changes a hypothesis and raises new ones. A useful side effect: once an event is written down with all four features, every empty feature is an explicit **knowledge gap** to work on.

blocks.code:
# Diamond events (SYNTHETIC). None = a feature we do not know yet.
events = [
    {"id": "E1", "adversary": None, "capability": "loader-X",
     "infrastructure": "update-check.example", "victim": "finance-laptop-7"},
    {"id": "E2", "adversary": None, "capability": "loader-X",
     "infrastructure": "203.0.113.80", "victim": "hr-laptop-2"},
    {"id": "E3", "adversary": None, "capability": "web-shell-Y",
     "infrastructure": "203.0.113.80", "victim": "web-server-1"},
    {"id": "E4", "adversary": None, "capability": "phish-kit-Z",
     "infrastructure": "login-portal.example", "victim": "sales-mail"},
]

def pivot(feature, value):
    return [e["id"] for e in events if e[feature] == value]

# Start from what the victim found: loader-X on finance-laptop-7
print("capability loader-X     :", pivot("capability", "loader-X"))
print("infrastructure 203...80 :", pivot("infrastructure", "203.0.113.80"))
gaps = [f for f in ("adversary", "capability", "infrastructure", "victim")
        if events[0][f] is None]
print("E1 knowledge gaps       :", gaps)

# Output:
# capability loader-X     : ['E1', 'E2']
# infrastructure 203...80 : ['E2', 'E3']
# E1 knowledge gaps       : ['adversary']
blocks.caption: Diamond events as records, and two pivots. Starting from loader-X on one laptop, the capability pivot finds a second victim, and the shared IP links that intrusion to a web-shell event on a server. Synthetic data.

blocks.md:
**From events to campaigns.** Events are phase-ordered into **activity threads**: for one adversary-victim pair, a directed graph of events whose arcs are labelled with confidence and marked as actual or hypothesised. Threads and events with shared features are then clustered into **activity groups**, built to answer a stated analytic problem (for example, "which intrusions share an operator?"). The paper's six-step process for groups runs: define the analytic problem, select features, create, grow, analyse, redefine.

The extended model adds a **social-political** meta-feature on the adversary-victim axis (what need does the victim satisfy for the adversary?) and a **technology** meta-feature on the capability-infrastructure axis. Victimology questions follow: why this victim, do the victims share a trait, who else might be next?

**Where analysts start.** The paper names "centered" approaches by starting corner:

- **Victim-centred**: what most organisations do, by monitoring their own networks. Honeypots (hosts set up to be attacked, as the Honeynet Project does) are a deliberate version.
- **Capability-centred**: start from malware, as antivirus vendors do; Kaspersky's "Red October" analysis pivoted from samples to over 1,000 related files, to infrastructure, to victims.
- **Infrastructure-centred**: start from domains and IPs; the paper cites an investigation that pivoted on domain registration details to find attacker domains before they were used.
- **Adversary-centred**: watch the adversary directly. The most fruitful and the rarest, because it needs access (the paper's example is the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) monitoring the "Phonemasters" group's phone calls).
- **Social-political-centred**: predict likely victims or adversaries from needs and motives, then watch there.

Two traps. First, Type 2 infrastructure is what victims usually see, so an IP address's owner is often another victim, not the adversary. Second, a shared feature is a lead, not a link: two events that share a widely used tool are not necessarily the same adversary (the attribution lesson returns to this).

blocks.question: A phishing email came from a real supplier's mailbox that attackers had taken over. In the Diamond Model, what is that mailbox?
options: Type 1 infrastructure, owned by the adversary
Type 2 infrastructure, controlled by an unwitting intermediary, and also a victim asset in an earlier event
The adversary feature
A capability
blocks.explain: The paper's Type 2 infrastructure includes compromised email accounts controlled by witting or unwitting intermediaries, and notes that a victim asset in one event can be leveraged as infrastructure in later events. Treating the supplier as the adversary would be a classic mistake.

blocks.question: Your endpoint detection tool found malware on one laptop and you have the C2 domain from reversing it. Which pivot is most likely to find other compromised machines in your own network?
options: Search DNS and proxy logs for other hosts that resolved or contacted the C2 domain and its IPs
Look up the adversary's motive
Check the malware's capacity against CVE lists
Wait for the attacker's next phishing email
blocks.explain: That is the infrastructure-to-victim pivot (pivot 4 in the paper's example): hosts talking to the same C2 infrastructure are candidate victims. It uses data you already hold, which is why victim-centred work starts there.

lessons.title: Kill chain and ATT&CK as analytic frames

blocks.md:
In *Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits* you met the intrusion kill chain (seven phases, break any link) and MITRE ATT&CK (tactics as the why, techniques as the how). Those were vocabularies. In CTI they become tools: for planning defences against a specific adversary, for linking intrusions into campaigns, and for comparing a threat report with what you can actually detect.

**Courses of action.** The 2011 kill chain paper maps each phase against six defensive actions taken from US Department of Defense information operations doctrine: **detect, deny, disrupt, degrade, deceive, destroy**. Its Table 1 is a *course of action matrix*. For the exploitation phase, for example, a host intrusion detection system (HIDS) can detect, patching denies, and data execution prevention (DEP) disrupts. Network intrusion detection and prevention systems (NIDS, NIPS) appear in several rows. "Here, completeness equates to resiliency."

blocks.title: The kill chain course of action matrix (paper's Table 1)

scenes.caption: Filled cells are where the paper's example lists a capability. Reading across a row shows how many ways you can act at that phase; reading down shows where one kind of action is missing.
Exploitation: HIDS detects, patching denies, DEP disrupts. Three independent ways to break one link.
Command and control has the most options: NIDS, firewall rules, NIPS, a tarpit to slow it, and DNS redirection to deceive the implant.
Nothing in the Destroy column: the paper's example lists no capability there. Each empty cell is a question to ask, not a rule.
Weaponization happens out of sight, yet the paper lists NIDS and NIPS there: its case study linked intrusions by identical weaponization traits in the delivered files.

blocks.md: **Campaign analysis and key indicators.** Analysing several intrusions side by side shows which indicators repeat across them. The paper calls the most consistent ones a campaign's **key indicators**: "centers of gravity" for defence, and the basis for linking new intrusions to known campaigns. It also makes a point about zero-days that every CTI analyst should keep: an adversary who spends a new exploit but "reuse[s] observable tools or infrastructure in other phases" is still caught if you hold mitigations for the repeated indicators. The goal, in the paper's words, is "less to positively attribute the identity of the intruders than to evaluate their capabilities, doctrine, objectives and limitations".

**ATT&CK as an intelligence source.** Beyond techniques, ATT&CK publishes entries for **groups** (IDs like G0016), **software** (S0365) and **campaigns** (C0024), each listing procedures with references to public reports. Two everyday uses:

- **Mapping a report**: tag each behaviour with a technique ID, so detection engineers read it in their own vocabulary. CISA advisories do this in an appendix.
- **Coverage comparison**: compare the techniques a relevant group uses with the techniques you have tested detections for. The gaps are your next detection or hunting work.

**Versions matter.** ATT&CK changes. The current release is v20.1, October 2026 (see the [versions page](https://attack.mitre.org/resources/versions/)). The old Defense Evasion tactic TA0005 is now named **Stealth**, a new **Defense Impairment** tactic (TA0112) has been added, and some technique IDs have moved: T1070.001, Clear Windows Event Logs, now redirects to T1685.005 under Disable or Modify Tools. A 2024 advisory mapped with v14 will not match a 2026 detection catalogue tagged with v20 unless you translate.

blocks.code:
# Techniques CISA AA24-038A (mapped with ATT&CK v14) lists for Volt Typhoon
advisory = {
    "T1190": "Exploit Public-Facing Application",
    "T1133": "External Remote Services",
    "T1078": "Valid Accounts",
    "T1021.001": "Remote Desktop Protocol",
    "T1047": "Windows Management Instrumentation",
    "T1003.003": "OS Credential Dumping: NTDS",
    "T1070.001": "Clear Windows Event Logs",
    "T1090.003": "Multi-hop Proxy",
}
# IDs that moved between ATT&CK versions (v14 to v20)
moved = {"T1070.001": "T1685.005"}
# Techniques our SIEM has a tested rule for, tagged with v20 IDs (SYNTHETIC)
ours = {"T1190", "T1021.001", "T1003.001", "T1059.001", "T1685.005"}

naive = advisory.keys() & ours
fixed = {moved.get(t, t) for t in advisory} & ours
print(f"naive match : {len(naive)} of {len(advisory)}")
print(f"after remap : {len(fixed)} of {len(advisory)}")
for t in sorted(advisory):
    if moved.get(t, t) not in ours:
        print("  gap:", t, advisory[t])

# Output:
# naive match : 2 of 8
# after remap : 3 of 8
#   gap: T1003.003 OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
#   gap: T1047 Windows Management Instrumentation
#   gap: T1078 Valid Accounts
#   gap: T1090.003 Multi-hop Proxy
#   gap: T1133 External Remote Services
blocks.caption: Comparing the techniques CISA AA24-038A maps for Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state-sponsored group that lesson 13 covers in full (a subset, ATT&CK v14), with a synthetic detection catalogue tagged with v20 IDs. Without remapping, a real detection is miscounted as a gap.

blocks.prompt: The naive comparison reported 2 of 8 techniques covered; after remapping, 3. What would have happened if nobody noticed?
blocks.reveal: The coverage report would show log clearing as a gap, and someone might spend a week writing a detection that already exists, while the real gaps (valid accounts over the VPN, theft of NTDS.dit (the Active Directory database file), WMI execution, proxy chains) wait. Worse, metrics built on mismatched versions drift silently. Record the ATT&CK version on every mapping, and translate IDs using the release notes or the redirects ATT&CK publishes before comparing.

blocks.md: Use the kill chain to ask "where can we act against this adversary, and how many independent ways?" and ATT&CK to ask "which of their known behaviours can we see?". Both answer defender decisions, which is why they belong in intelligence products.

blocks.question: An adversary uses a new zero-day exploit but the same command-and-control domains and the same mail-theft tool as last year. According to the kill chain paper, what does that mean for a well-prepared defender?
options: Nothing can stop a zero-day, so the intrusion succeeds
The defender must first attribute the zero-day to a country
Mitigations for the repeated indicators in other phases can still break the chain
Only patching can help
blocks.explain: The paper argues the exploit 'is but one change in a broader process': if intruders reuse tools or infrastructure in other phases, defenders holding mitigations for those indicators still stop the intrusion. That is the value of complete, multi-phase coverage.

blocks.question: A 2024 advisory tags log clearing as T1070.001. Your 2026 detection list (ATT&CK v20) has a rule tagged T1685.005. What is the right conclusion?
options: They are unrelated techniques
They describe the same behaviour under different ATT&CK versions; translate the ID before measuring coverage
The advisory is wrong
T1685.005 must be deprecated
blocks.explain: In ATT&CK v20, T1070.001 Clear Windows Event Logs redirects to T1685.005 under Disable or Modify Tools. Mappings are version-specific, so compare like with like.

lessons.title: STIX 2.1: threat intelligence as a graph

blocks.md:
Your team writes: "domain update-check.example indicates LoaderX; LoaderX is used by cluster UNC-EXAMPLE-1; we saw the domain three times; confidence moderate; share with the community". A human reads that in five seconds. A partner's SIEM cannot read it at all, and if each partner retypes it, errors creep in. Machine-to-machine sharing needs an agreed structure.

**STIX** (Structured Threat Information Expression) is that structure: a language and serialization format for CTI. Version 2.1 became an **OASIS Standard** on 10 June 2021; OASIS is a standards consortium, and its CTI Technical Committee (the 2.1 specification names chairs from MITRE and CERT.be, Belgium's national computer emergency response team) maintains STIX and its transport protocol TAXII (next lesson). STIX 2.1 serialises to JSON.

**A connected graph.** The specification says it plainly: "STIX is a connected graph of nodes and edges". The node types:

- **SDOs** (STIX Domain Objects): the analyst's concepts. The overview lists 18 (section 4 also defines a stub Incident object): Attack Pattern, Campaign, Course of Action, Grouping, Identity, Indicator, Infrastructure, Intrusion Set, Location, Malware, Malware Analysis, Note, Observed Data, Opinion, Report, Threat Actor, Tool and Vulnerability.
- **SCOs** (STIX Cyber-observable Objects): facts seen on hosts and networks, such as a file, a domain name or network traffic, which "do not capture the who, when, or why".

The edges are **SROs** (STIX Relationship Objects): the generic **Relationship**, whose `relationship_type` is a verb such as `indicates`, `uses` or `attributed-to`, and the **Sighting**, which records that someone saw something and how often. **Bundles** wrap objects for transport, and **marking definitions** carry handling rules such as TLP.

**Three easily confused SDOs.**

- **Campaign**: "a set of malicious activities or attacks ... that occur over a period of time against a specific set of targets", usually with well-defined objectives.
- **Intrusion Set**: "a grouped set of adversarial behaviors and resources with common properties that is believed to be orchestrated by a single organization". Activity can be attributed to an intrusion set "even if the Threat Actors behind the attack are not known". Mandiant's UNC clusters and named APT groups map naturally here.
- **Threat Actor**: "actual individuals, groups, or organizations believed to be operating with malicious intent".

So the usual chain is campaign `attributed-to` intrusion set `attributed-to` threat actor, and each link can carry its own `confidence` (0 to 100).

blocks.title: A small STIX 2.1 bundle as a graph

scenes.caption: The indicator holds a detection pattern, [domain-name:value = 'update-check.example'], plus validity dates and a confidence.
A Relationship object of type indicates links it to the Malware object. The edge is its own object, so it can carry its own confidence and author.
The intrusion set uses the malware. New intrusions using LoaderX can now be linked to the cluster even though nobody knows who is behind it.
A Sighting records that the SOC (an Identity) saw the indicator 3 times. Sightings are how producers learn which indicators fire.
Embedded references such as object_marking_refs point at a TLP marking. The dashed attributed-to? edge marks a gap: leave it out of the bundle until there is evidence.

blocks.code:
from stix2 import (Bundle, Identity, Indicator, IntrusionSet, Malware,
                   Relationship, Sighting, TLP_GREEN)

soc = Identity(name="Example Corp SOC", identity_class="organization")
loader = Malware(name="LoaderX", is_family=True)
group = IntrusionSet(name="UNC-EXAMPLE-1", confidence=50)
ind = Indicator(
    name="LoaderX C2 domain",
    pattern="[domain-name:value = 'update-check.example']",
    pattern_type="stix", valid_from="2026-11-13T00:00:00Z",
    confidence=70, object_marking_refs=[TLP_GREEN], created_by_ref=soc)

bundle = Bundle(soc, loader, group, ind,
                Relationship(ind, "indicates", loader),
                Relationship(group, "uses", loader),
                Sighting(sighting_of_ref=ind, where_sighted_refs=[soc], count=3))

name = {o.id: o.get("name", o.type) for o in bundle.objects}
for o in bundle.objects:
    if o.type == "relationship":
        print("edge:", name[o.source_ref], f"[{o.relationship_type}]", name[o.target_ref])
    elif o.type == "sighting":
        print("edge:", name[o.sighting_of_ref], f"[seen x{o.count}]", "by", name[o.where_sighted_refs[0]])
    else:
        print("node:", o.type, "|", o.name)

# Output:
# node: identity | Example Corp SOC
# node: malware | LoaderX
# node: intrusion-set | UNC-EXAMPLE-1
# node: indicator | LoaderX C2 domain
# edge: LoaderX C2 domain [indicates] LoaderX
# edge: UNC-EXAMPLE-1 [uses] LoaderX
# edge: LoaderX C2 domain [seen x3] by Example Corp SOC
blocks.caption: Building the same bundle with the OASIS stix2 Python library (version 3.0.2). IDs are random UUIDs, so the script prints types and names rather than IDs.

blocks.md:
**Rules worth knowing.** Every object has `type`, `spec_version`, `id`, `created` and `modified`; an ID is the type, two hyphens and a UUID, for example `indicator--` followed by 36 characters. An Indicator also requires `pattern`, `pattern_type` and `valid_from`; the pattern may be STIX patterning or "another appropriate language such as SNORT, YARA". References that are an inherent fact of an object, such as `created_by_ref`, are **embedded relationships**, and only the object's creator can assert them; anything a third party might add, or that needs its own confidence, is a separate Relationship.

**A version mismatch to watch.** STIX 2.1's built-in TLP marking definitions are the four TLP 1.0 labels: WHITE, GREEN, AMBER and RED. FIRST's current [TLP 2.0](https://www.first.org/tlp/) (authoritative from August 2022) labels are RED, AMBER (with an AMBER+STRICT variant), GREEN and CLEAR, so CLEAR and AMBER+STRICT have no built-in STIX 2.1 definition. The OASIS CTI TC publishes TLP 2.0 markings as a STIX extension; check which form your tools accept before trusting a marking.

STIX makes sharing easy, including sharing mistakes. A wrong `attributed-to` edge, or an indicator without `valid_until` and confidence, propagates to every consumer automatically. Model uncertainty explicitly: use confidence, Opinion objects, and leave edges out when evidence is missing.

blocks.question: You have linked twelve intrusions by shared tooling and infrastructure but have no idea who is behind them. Which STIX object fits the cluster?
options: Threat Actor
Identity
Observed Data
Intrusion Set
blocks.explain: STIX defines an Intrusion Set as grouped adversarial behaviours and resources believed to be orchestrated by a single organisation, and allows activity to be attributed to it even when the Threat Actors are not known. A Threat Actor object asserts actual individuals or organisations.

blocks.question: Which properties must every STIX 2.1 Indicator have in addition to the common ones (type, spec_version, id, created, modified)?
options: name and description
confidence and labels
pattern, pattern_type and valid_from
kill_chain_phases
blocks.explain: The specification marks pattern, pattern_type and valid_from as required for Indicator. name and description are optional (producers SHOULD provide them), and confidence is an optional common property.

lessons.title: Sharing at machine speed: TAXII, MISP and communities

blocks.md:
STIX describes the intelligence; something still has to move it. In December 2020, a few days after the SolarWinds compromise became public, CISA updated its advisory [AA20-352A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa20-352a) and "provided a downloadable STIX file of the IOCs". A file on a web page works, but every consumer has to notice the update, download it and load it. Sharing at scale needs a protocol that machines can poll, and platforms where analysts can work on the shared data together.

**TAXII** (Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information) is the protocol: in the words of the TAXII 2.1 specification (an OASIS Standard, also 10 June 2021), "an application layer protocol used to exchange cyber threat intelligence (CTI) over HTTPS". It is designed for STIX but not limited to it.

**TAXII 2.1 in five ideas.**

- **Discovery**: a server describes itself at `/taxii2/` (or is advertised with a DNS SRV record), listing its **API Roots**.
- **API Roots** are separate instances of the API at different URLs, so one server can host, for example, one root per trust group with its own access control.
- **Collections**: "an interface to a logical repository of CTI objects". Clients GET objects from `{api-root}/collections/{id}/objects/` and POST new ones to the same URL; a status endpoint reports whether a POST was accepted.
- **Channels** (publish-subscribe) are named in the specification but their services are left to a future version.
- **Content negotiation**: requests and responses use the media type `application/taxii+json;version=2.1`. Polling clients pass `added_after` to fetch only what is new since their last request.

blocks.title: A TAXII 2.1 client polling a collection

scenes.caption: Discovery: the client asks the server what it offers and gets a list of API Roots it may use.
It lists the collections in its trust group's API Root and picks one, say the sector's high-confidence indicators.
Each poll asks only for objects added since the last poll. The response is an envelope of STIX objects.
The client converts usable indicators into SIEM lookups, with their confidence and valid_until dates, so they can age out.
Sharing back: the client POSTs a Sighting to the collection, if the API Root allows writes, and checks the status endpoint.

GET /api1/collections/91a7b528-80eb-42ed-a74d-c6fbd5a26116/objects/?added_after=2026-11-12T00:00:00Z HTTP/1.1
Host: taxii.example.org
Accept: application/taxii+json;version=2.1
Authorization: Basic <redacted>

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/taxii+json;version=2.1
X-TAXII-Date-Added-First: 2026-11-12T08:14:03.000Z
X-TAXII-Date-Added-Last: 2026-11-13T07:02:41.000Z

{"more": false, "objects": [ { "type": "indicator", "spec_version": "2.1", ... } ]}
